transcription.tex: Both models count events. What fixes the possible values of each count?
Binomial model
Poisson model
$X\sim\operatorname{B}(n,p)$
$Y\sim\operatorname{Po}(\lambda)$
Count successes in $n$ independent trials. Each trial has two outcomes and the same probability $p$ of success.
Possible counts: $0,1,\ldots,n$. At most $n$ trials can succeed.
Count events in a fixed interval. The parameter $\lambda$ (“lambda”) is the expected number of events in that interval.
Possible counts: $0,1,2,\ldots$. There is no fixed upper bound.

slides.title: Modelling car arrivals in ten intervals

transcription.tex: The Poisson distribution gives the probability of a particular count in a fixed interval when events occur independently at a constant average rate.
Calculate the probability of 8 cars passing in the next hour, given that on average 5 pass an hour.
First try a binomial model. Divide the hour into ten six-minute intervals and allow at most one car per interval.

shapes.alt: Ten six-minute intervals from 2 pm to 3 pm. Ticks in intervals 1, 4, 5, 8 and 10.

transcription.tex: Each tick represents one interval with a car. This example shows five occupied intervals. The question asks about eight.
Match the mean of five cars per hour: \(10p=5\), so \(p=5/10=0.5\).
For ten independent trials, \(X\sim\mathrm{B}(10,0.5)\).\par \(P(X=8)=\binom{10}{8}(0.5)^8(0.5)^2=0.0439\) (4 d.p.). This is the ten-interval approximation.
Two cars can pass in the same interval. Counting that interval only once would undercount the cars. How could we lessen this problem?
Ten intervals of six minutes. Five are occupied.
Twenty intervals of three minutes. Two arrivals previously in the same interval can now be distinguished.
With twenty intervals and the same mean of five cars per hour, calculate the probability of eight cars passing.

\(20p=5\), so \(p=0.25\) and \(X\sim\mathrm{B}(20,0.25)\).\par \(P(X=8)=\binom{20}{8}(0.25)^8(0.75)^{12}=0.0609\) (4 d.p.).\par As the intervals get shorter, two or more arrivals in a single interval become less likely.

transcription.tex: We saw with in order to model something with a Binomial Distribution, we had to make some assumptions, e.g. each event was independent, and had two outcomes.\par We have similar restrictions on events for a Poisson Distribution:
Events occur singly in time. Treat arrivals as instantaneous.
The number of events in disjoint intervals is independent. An arrival just now does not change the chance of another arrival in the next interval.
The expected count is proportional to the interval length. The word “rate” is a clue in exam questions. Check that the assumptions fit the situation.

A website receives hits at a rate of 300 per hour.
(a) State a distribution that is suitable to model the number of hits obtained during a 1 minute interval.
(b) State two reasons for your answer to part (a).
Jan 2012 Q4
In one minute the mean is \(300/60=5\). Use \(X\sim\operatorname{Po}(5)\).
Hits occur singly, independently and at a constant rate. Any two of these properties justify the model.

slides.title: When is a Poisson model suitable?

transcription.tex: Which counts could reasonably be modelled by a Poisson distribution? Explain using the assumptions.

shapes.alt: A volcanic cone ejects lava and ash at dusk.

transcription.tex: A volcano erupts every 1000 years, and we’re interested in the probability of at least one eruption next year.
If that interval is regular, a Poisson model is unsuitable. Even if 1000 years is only an average, the recent eruption history may change the chance of another eruption.

shapes.alt: A red route 281 double-decker arriving at a bus stop.

transcription.tex: On average the 281 bus comes 10 times an hour. We’re interested in the probability of (at least one) bus coming in the next hour.
A timetable puts buses about six minutes apart. Arrivals are more likely near scheduled times, so a constant-rate Poisson model is unsuitable.

shapes.alt: Two call-centre operators at their workstations wearing headsets.

transcription.tex: A call centre receives on average 80 calls an hour, and wish to work out the probability they have over 100 calls at some hour in the day.
Plausible for a particular hour if calls arrive independently at a steady rate. Repeat calls or busy times could break those assumptions.

Defects occur at random in planks of wood with a constant rate of 0.5 per 10 cm length. Jim buys a plank of length 100 cm.
(a) Find the probability that Jim’s plank contains at most 3 defects.
Shivani buys 6 planks each of length 100 cm.
(b) Find the probability that fewer than 2 of Shivani’s planks contain at most 3 defects.
May 2011 Q5
The mean is 0.5 defects per 10 cm, hence 5 per plank. With \(X\sim\operatorname{Po}(5)\), \(P(X\le3)=0.2650\).
Let \(Y\) count the planks containing at most 3 defects. For six independent planks, \(Y\sim\operatorname{B}(6,0.2650)\).\par \(P(Y<2)=P(Y=0)+P(Y=1)\)\par \(=0.735^6+6(0.265)(0.735)^5=0.4987\ldots\).

Think carefully about whether we wish to use Binomial or Poisson. You should be clear about what your random variables are and how they’re distributed. Sometimes we need to scale the rate to a different time period/length.

transcription.tex: Question 7

An estate agent has been selling houses at a rate of 1.8 per week.\par \textbf{a} Find the probability that in a particular week she sells:\par (i) no houses     (ii) 3 houses     (iii) at least 3 houses.\par The estate agent meets her weekly target if she sells at least 3 houses in one week.\par \textbf{b} Find the probability that over a period of 4 consecutive weeks she meets her weekly target exactly once.\par \textbf{Problem-solving} Use a binomial model for part b.

\textbf{a} Let $X$ count the houses she sells in one week. Then $X\sim\operatorname{Po}(1.8)$. Use the Poisson formula or a calculator with $\lambda=1.8$.\par (i) $\mathrm P(X=0)=\dfrac{e^{-1.8}1.8^0}{0!}=0.1653$ (4 d.p.).\par (ii) $\mathrm P(X=3)=\dfrac{e^{-1.8}1.8^3}{3!}=0.1607$ (4 d.p.).\par (iii) $\mathrm P(X\ge3)=1-\mathrm P(X\le2)=1-0.7306=0.2694$.\par \textbf{b} Let $Y$ count the weeks in which she meets her target. In each of four independent weeks the probability of success is $p=\mathrm P(X\ge3)$ from (a)(iii). Thus $Y\sim\operatorname{B}(4,p)$.\par $\mathrm P(Y=1)=\binom41p(1-p)^3=0.4202$ (4 d.p.).
Question 8

Patients arrive at a hospital accident and emergency department at random at a rate of 5 per hour.\par \textbf{a} Find the probability that, during any 30-minute period, the number of patients arriving at the hospital accident and emergency department is:\par (i) exactly 4     (ii) at least 3.\par A patient arrives at 11:00 am.\par \textbf{b} Find the probability that the next patient arrives before 11:15 am.

\textbf{a} Let $X$ count arrivals in 30 minutes. The mean is $5\times\frac12=2.5$, so $X\sim\operatorname{Po}(2.5)$.\par (i) $\mathrm P(X=4)=\dfrac{e^{-2.5}2.5^4}{4!}=0.1336$ (4 d.p.).\par (ii) From the Poisson tables with $\lambda=2.5$,\par $\mathrm P(X\ge3)=1-\mathrm P(X\le2)=1-0.5438=0.4562$.\par \textbf{b} The next patient arrives before 11:15 am precisely when there is at least one further arrival in those 15 minutes. Let $Y$ count these arrivals.\par The mean is $5\times\frac14=1.25$, so $Y\sim\operatorname{Po}(1.25)$. Using a calculator,\par $\mathrm P(Y\ge1)=1-\mathrm P(Y=0)=1-e^{-1.25}=1-0.2865=0.7135$.
Question 9

The lift in a block of flats breaks down at random at a mean rate of three times per four-week period.\par \textbf{a} Find the probability that the lift breaks down:\par (i) at least once in one week\par (ii) exactly twice in one week.\par In one particular week, the lift broke down twice.\par \textbf{b} Write down the probability that the lift will break down at some point in the next week. Give a reason for your answer.

\textbf{a} Let $X$ count the breakdowns in one week. The weekly mean is $3/4=0.75$, so $X\sim\operatorname{Po}(0.75)$. Use a calculator.\par (i) $\mathrm P(X\ge1)=1-\mathrm P(X=0)=1-e^{-0.75}=1-0.4724=0.5276$.\par (ii) $\mathrm P(X=2)=\dfrac{e^{-0.75}0.75^2}{2!}=0.1329$ (4 d.p.).\par \textbf{b} In the Poisson model, counts in disjoint weeks are independent. The two breakdowns last week leave the probability for next week unchanged. From (a)(i) the probability is $0.5276$.
Question 10

Flaws occur at random in a particular type of material at a mean rate of 1.5 per 50 m.\par \textbf{a} Find the probability that, in a randomly chosen 50 m length of this material, there will be exactly 3 flaws.\par This material is sold in rolls of length 200 m.\par \textbf{b} Find the probability that a single roll has fewer than 4 flaws.\par Priya buys 5 rolls of this material.\par \textbf{c} Find the probability that at least two of these rolls will have fewer than 4 flaws.

\textbf{a} Let $X$ count the flaws in 50 m. Then $X\sim\operatorname{Po}(1.5)$.\par $\mathrm P(X=3)=\dfrac{e^{-1.5}1.5^3}{3!}=0.1255$ (4 d.p.).\par \textbf{b} Let $Y$ count the flaws in 200 m. The mean is $4(1.5)=6$, so $Y\sim\operatorname{Po}(6)$. From the tables, $p=\mathrm P(Y<4)=\mathrm P(Y\le3)=0.1512$ (4 d.p.).\par \textbf{c} Let $A$ count the rolls with fewer than 4 flaws. With five independent rolls, $A\sim\operatorname{B}(5,p)$.\par $\mathrm P(A\ge2)=1-\mathrm P(A=1)-\mathrm P(A=0)$\par $=1-\binom51p(1-p)^4-\binom50p^0(1-p)^5=0.1670$ (using the tabulated $p=0.1512$).
Question 11

A company produces chocolate chip biscuits. The number of chocolate chips per biscuit has a Poisson distribution with mean 5.\par \textbf{a} Find the probability that one of these biscuits, selected at random, contains fewer than 3 chocolate chips.\par A packet contains 6 of these biscuits, selected at random.\par \textbf{b} Find the probability that exactly half of the biscuits in the packet contain fewer than 3 chocolate chips.

\textbf{a} Let $X$ count the chips in one biscuit, so $X\sim\operatorname{Po}(5)$. From the tables with $\lambda=5$,\par $p=\mathrm P(X<3)=\mathrm P(X\le2)=0.1247$ (4 d.p.).\par \textbf{b} Let $Y$ count the biscuits in the packet that contain fewer than 3 chips. With six independently selected biscuits, $Y\sim\operatorname{B}(6,p)$.\par Exactly half of six means three biscuits.\par $\mathrm P(Y=3)=\binom63p^3(1-p)^3=0.0260$ (4 d.p.).
Question 12

A company has minibuses that can only be hired for a week at a time. All hiring starts on a Sunday. During the summer, the mean number of requests for minibuses each Sunday is 5.\par \textbf{a} Calculate the probability that fewer than 4 requests for minibuses are made on a particular Sunday in summer.\par The company wants to be at least 99% sure they can fulfil all requests on any particular Sunday.\par \textbf{b} Calculate the number of minibuses the company must have in order to satisfy this condition.

\textbf{a} Let $X$ count requests on a summer Sunday. Model $X\sim\operatorname{Po}(5)$. From the tables with $\lambda=5$,\par $\mathrm P(X<4)=\mathrm P(X\le3)=0.2650$.\par \textbf{b} Let $n$ be the fleet size. The company can fulfil all requests whenever $X\le n$, so choose the smallest integer $n$ with $\mathrm P(X\le n)\ge0.99$.\par $\mathrm P(X\le10)=0.9863<0.99$.\par $\mathrm P(X\le11)=0.9945\ge0.99$.\par The company needs 11 minibuses.
Question 13

On a typical summer’s day, a boat company hires out rowing boats at a rate of 9 per hour.\par \textbf{a} Find the probability of hiring out at least 6 boats in a randomly selected 30-minute period.\par The company has 8 boats and decides to hire them out for 20-minute periods.\par \textbf{b} Show that the probability of running out of boats is less than 1%.\par \textbf{c} Find the number of boats that the company should have in order to be 99% sure of meeting all demands if the hire period is extended to 30 minutes.

\textbf{a} Let $X$ count hires in 30 minutes. The mean is $9/2=4.5$, so $X\sim\operatorname{Po}(4.5)$. From the tables,\par $\mathrm P(X\ge6)=1-\mathrm P(X\le5)=1-0.7029=0.2971$.\par \textbf{b} Let $Y$ count requests in 20 minutes. The mean is $9/3=3$, so $Y\sim\operatorname{Po}(3)$. A request goes unmet when there are more than eight requests.\par $\mathrm P(Y>8)=1-\mathrm P(Y\le8)=1-0.9962=0.0038$.\par This is $0.38\%$, which is less than $1\%$.\par \textbf{c} For 30 minutes use $X\sim\operatorname{Po}(4.5)$ again. Find the smallest fleet size $n$ with $\mathrm P(X\le n)\ge0.99$.\par $\mathrm P(X\le9)=0.9829<0.99$, while $\mathrm P(X\le10)=0.9933\ge0.99$.\par The company needs 10 boats.
Question 14

Breakdowns on a particular machine occur at a rate of 1.5 per week.\par \textbf{a} Find the probability that no more than 2 breakdowns occur in a randomly chosen week.\par \textbf{b} Find the probability of at least 5 breakdowns in a randomly chosen two-week period.\par A maintenance firm offers a contract for repairing breakdowns over a six-week period. The firm will give a full refund if there are more than $n$ breakdowns in a six-week period.\par The firm wants the probability of having to pay a refund to be 5% or less.\par \textbf{c} Find the smallest possible value of $n$.

\textbf{a} Let $X$ count breakdowns in a week, so $X\sim\operatorname{Po}(1.5)$. From the tables, $\mathrm P(X\le2)=0.8088$.\par \textbf{b} Let $Y$ count breakdowns in two weeks. Then $Y\sim\operatorname{Po}(3)$. The complement of “at least 5” is “at most 4”.\par $\mathrm P(Y\ge5)=1-\mathrm P(Y\le4)=1-0.8153=0.1847$.\par \textbf{c} Let $A$ count breakdowns in six weeks. The mean is $6(1.5)=9$, so $A\sim\operatorname{Po}(9)$.\par A refund is due when $A>n$. We require $\mathrm P(A>n)\le0.05$.\par Since $\mathrm P(A>n)=1-\mathrm P(A\le n)$, this is equivalent to $\mathrm P(A\le n)\ge0.95$.\par With mean 9, $\mathrm P(A\le13)=0.9261<0.95$ and $\mathrm P(A\le14)=0.9585\ge0.95$.\par Therefore the smallest possible value is $n=14$.
Prerequisite: Year 2 conditional probability.

In a football game of France versus Croatia, France score goals at a rate of \(\lambda\) per 10 minutes. Given that in a (90 minute) game France score 5 goals, determine the probability that 2 of those goals were scored within the first 10 minutes.

Let \(X\) count goals in the first 10 minutes and \(Y\) in the remaining 80. The intervals are disjoint, so the counts are independent.\par \(X\sim\mathrm{Po}(\lambda),\quad Y\sim\mathrm{Po}(8\lambda),\quad X+Y\sim\mathrm{Po}(9\lambda).\)\par Five goals in total and two in the first ten minutes mean three in the remaining eighty.\par \(\displaystyle P(X=2\mid X+Y=5)=\frac{P(X=2,Y=3)}{P(X+Y=5)}=\frac{P(X=2)P(Y=3)}{P(X+Y=5)}\)\par \(\displaystyle =\frac{(e^{-\lambda}\lambda^2/2!)(e^{-8\lambda}(8\lambda)^3/3!)}{e^{-9\lambda}(9\lambda)^5/5!}=\frac{5!}{2!\,3!}\frac{8^3}{9^5}=\boxed{\frac{5120}{59049}}.\)
Two fair three-sided spinners are spun independently. Let $X$ and $Y$ be their scores. Each spinner has three equally likely outcomes.

transcription.tex: $\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|}\hline x&1&2&3\\\hline p(x)&\tfrac13&\tfrac13&\tfrac13\\\hline\end{array}$

shapes.alt: Three-sided spinner with blue, green and red faces labelled 2, 3, 4.

transcription.tex: $\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|}\hline y&2&3&4\\\hline p(y)&\tfrac13&\tfrac13&\tfrac13\\\hline\end{array}$
Let $Z=X+Y$. Add the two spinner scores for each of the nine equally likely pairs.
$\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|}\hline x\backslash y&2&3&4\\\hline 1&3&4&5\\\hline 2&4&5&6\\\hline 3&5&6&7\\\hline\end{array}$

$\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline z&3&4&5&6&7\\\hline p(z)&\tfrac{1}{9}&\tfrac{2}{9}&\tfrac{3}{9}&\tfrac{2}{9}&\tfrac{1}{9}\\\hline\end{array}$\par Only $3+4$ gives 7. The five probabilities sum to 1.
Independence gives every ordered pair probability $\tfrac13\times\tfrac13=\tfrac19$.

parts.text: If 5 cars pass per hour in road A and 8 cars pass per hour in road B, how many cars pass per hour in roads A and B combined?

Obviously 13 per hour! This suggests that if we have two independent Poisson counts and want to represent the total number of events across the same time interval, we can form a new Poisson distribution in which we simply add the rates.

transcription.tex: Question 6

A taxi company supplies two particular organisations independently.\par Company A orders taxis at a rate of 1.25 cars per day.\par Company B orders taxis at a rate of 0.75 cars per day.\par \textbf{a} On a given day, find the probability that 2 cars are ordered by company A.\par \textbf{b} On a given day, find the probability that the total number of cars ordered by both companies is 2.\par \textbf{c} In a given 5-day working week, find the probability that the total number of cars ordered by both companies is less than 10.

Let $A$ and $B$ be the daily numbers ordered by the two companies. The counts are independent, with $A\sim\operatorname{Po}(1.25)$ and $B\sim\operatorname{Po}(0.75)$.\par \textbf{a} $\mathrm P(A=2)=\dfrac{e^{-1.25}1.25^2}{2!}=0.2238$ (4 d.p.).\par \textbf{b} Add the means of the independent Poisson variables. $A+B\sim\operatorname{Po}(1.25+0.75)=\operatorname{Po}(2)$.\par $\mathrm P(A+B=2)=\dfrac{e^{-2}2^2}{2!}=0.2707$ (4 d.p.).\par \textbf{c} Let $C$ be the total number of taxis ordered in five days. Its mean is $5\times2=10$, so $C\sim\operatorname{Po}(10)$. From the tables, $\mathrm P(C<10)=\mathrm P(C\le9)=0.4579$.
Question 7

A restaurant has two coffee machines, $C$ and $D$. Machine $C$ breaks down at a rate of 0.1 times per week while, independently, machine $D$ breaks down at a rate of 0.05 times per week.\par Find the probability that, in a 12-week period,\par \textbf{a} machine $C$ breaks down at least once\par \textbf{b} each machine breaks down at least once\par \textbf{c} there will be a total of 3 breakdowns.

Write $C$ and $D$ for the respective numbers of breakdowns in 12 weeks. Their means are $12(0.1)=1.2$ and $12(0.05)=0.6$. The counts are independent.\par \textbf{a} $C\sim\operatorname{Po}(1.2)$. Using a calculator,\par $\mathrm P(C\ge1)=1-\mathrm P(C=0)=1-\dfrac{e^{-1.2}1.2^0}{0!}=1-0.3012=0.6988$.\par \textbf{b} $D\sim\operatorname{Po}(0.6)$. Independence gives\par $\mathrm P(C\ge1,D\ge1)=\mathrm P(C\ge1)\mathrm P(D\ge1)$\par $=0.6988\left(1-\dfrac{e^{-0.6}0.6^0}{0!}\right)\approx0.6988(1-0.5488)$\par $\approx0.6988\times0.4512=0.3153$ (4 d.p.).\par \textbf{c} $C+D\sim\operatorname{Po}(1.2+0.6)=\operatorname{Po}(1.8)$. Using a calculator,\par $\mathrm P(C+D=3)=\dfrac{e^{-1.8}1.8^3}{3!}=0.1607$ (4 d.p.).
Question 8

A secretary receives internal calls at a rate of 1 every 5 minutes and external calls at a rate of 2 every 5 minutes.\par Calculate the probability that the total number of calls is:\par \textbf{a} 3 in a 4-minute period\par \textbf{b} at least 2 in a 2-minute period\par \textbf{c} no more than 5 in a 10-minute period.

Model the two streams of calls as independent Poisson processes. The combined rate is $1+2=3$ calls per 5 minutes.\par \textbf{a} Let $A$ count calls in 4 minutes. Its mean is $3(4/5)=2.4$, so $A\sim\operatorname{Po}(2.4)$.\par $\mathrm P(A=3)=\dfrac{e^{-2.4}2.4^3}{3!}=0.2090$ (4 d.p.).\par \textbf{b} Let $B$ count calls in 2 minutes. Its mean is $3(2/5)=1.2$, so $B\sim\operatorname{Po}(1.2)$.\par $\mathrm P(B\ge2)=1-\mathrm P(B\le1)=1-\mathrm P(B=0)-\mathrm P(B=1)$\par $=1-\dfrac{e^{-1.2}1.2^0}{0!}-\dfrac{e^{-1.2}1.2^1}{1!}\approx1-0.30119-0.36143=0.3374$ (4 d.p.).\par \textbf{c} Let $C$ count calls in 10 minutes. Its mean is $3(10/5)=6$. From the tables for $C\sim\operatorname{Po}(6)$, $\mathrm P(C\le5)=0.4457$.
Question 9

An office is situated on 3 floors of a building. On each floor it has a photocopier. The ground-floor photocopier breaks down at a rate of 0.4 times per week, the first-floor photocopier breaks down at a rate of 0.2 times per week and the second-floor photocopier breaks down at a rate of 0.8 times per week. Find the probability, in a given week, that:\par \textbf{a} each photocopier will break down exactly once\par \textbf{b} at least one photocopier breaks down\par \textbf{c} there will be a total of 2 breakdowns.

Let $A$, $B$ and $C$ count breakdowns on the ground, first and second floors respectively. Model them as independent Poisson variables with means $0.4$, $0.2$ and $0.8$.\par \textbf{a} By independence, $\mathrm P(A=1,B=1,C=1)=\mathrm P(A=1)\mathrm P(B=1)\mathrm P(C=1)$.\par $=\dfrac{e^{-0.4}0.4^1}{1!}\dfrac{e^{-0.2}0.2^1}{1!}\dfrac{e^{-0.8}0.8^1}{1!}$\par $\approx0.26813\times0.16375\times0.35946=0.0158$ (4 d.p.).\par \textbf{b} The total $T=A+B+C$ has distribution $\operatorname{Po}(0.4+0.2+0.8)=\operatorname{Po}(1.4)$. Using a calculator,\par $\mathrm P(T\ge1)=1-\mathrm P(T=0)=1-\dfrac{e^{-1.4}1.4^0}{0!}\approx1-0.2466=0.7534$.\par \textbf{c} $\mathrm P(T=2)=\dfrac{e^{-1.4}1.4^2}{2!}=0.2417$ (4 d.p.).
Question 10

During the working day the emails arriving to the account of a company director are classified into three types: personal, business and advertising. Personal emails arrive at a mean rate of 1.8 per hour, business emails arrive at a mean rate of 3.7 per hour and advertising emails arrive at a mean rate of 1.5 per hour. Find the probability that she receives:\par \textbf{a} at least one of each type of email during a 30-minute period of the working day\par \textbf{b} more than 50 emails in an 8-hour working day.\par \textbf{c} Find the probability that she receives more than 50 emails on exactly two days out of a 5-day working week.\par \textbf{Hint} Use a binomial model for part c.

\textbf{a} Let $A$, $B$ and $C$ count personal, business and advertising emails in half an hour. Assume independent Poisson counts. Their means are $1.8/2=0.9$, $3.7/2=1.85$ and $1.5/2=0.75$.\par $\mathrm P(A\ge1,B\ge1,C\ge1)$\par $=[1-\mathrm P(A=0)][1-\mathrm P(B=0)][1-\mathrm P(C=0)]$\par $=\left(1-\dfrac{e^{-0.9}0.9^0}{0!}\right)\left(1-\dfrac{e^{-1.85}1.85^0}{0!}\right)\left(1-\dfrac{e^{-0.75}0.75^0}{0!}\right)$\par $\approx(1-0.4066)(1-0.1572)(1-0.4724)$\par $\approx0.5934\times0.8428\times0.5276=0.2639$ (4 d.p.).\par \textbf{b} Let $D$ count emails in 8 hours. The total rate is $1.8+3.7+1.5=7$ per hour, so $D\sim\operatorname{Po}(8\times7)=\operatorname{Po}(56)$.\par $p=\mathrm P(D>50)=1-\mathrm P(D\le50)\approx1-0.2343=0.7657$.\par \textbf{c} Let $X$ count the days with more than 50 emails. Over five independent days, $X\sim\operatorname{B}(5,p)$ using $p$ from (b).\par $\mathrm P(X=2)=\binom52(0.7657)^2(1-0.7657)^3=0.0754$ (4 d.p.).

slides.title: Mean and variance of a Poisson count

transcription.tex: For $X\sim\operatorname{Po}(\lambda)$, what is the expected count in the interval? How does its variance compare?
$\mathrm E(X)=\lambda,\qquad\operatorname{Var}(X)=\lambda$. Compare the sample mean and variance when assessing a Poisson model.
Derive the mean from the probability function.

$\mathrm E(X)=\sum_{x=0}^{\infty}x\,\mathrm P(X=x)=\sum_{x=0}^{\infty}\dfrac{x\,e^{-\lambda}\lambda^x}{x!}$.\par The term for $x=0$ vanishes. For $x\ge1$, use $x/x!=1/(x-1)!$.\par $\mathrm E(X)=e^{-\lambda}\sum_{x=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{x\lambda^x}{x!}=\lambda e^{-\lambda}\sum_{x=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{\lambda^{x-1}}{(x-1)!}$.

Put $j=x-1$. The sum now starts at $j=0$.\par $\displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\dfrac{\lambda^j}{j!}=1+\dfrac{\lambda}{1!}+\dfrac{\lambda^2}{2!}+\cdots=e^\lambda$.\par Hence $\mathrm E(X)=\lambda e^{-\lambda}e^\lambda=\lambda$.
The exponential series is studied in Core Pure Year 2. Later in Further Statistics, a probability generating function gives another route.

transcription.tex: Question 3

\textbf{a} Calculate the mean and the variance of the data.\par \textbf{b} Explain why the results in part a suggest that a Poisson distribution may be a suitable model for the number of flaws on a piece of cloth.\par The factory produces 10 000 pieces of cloth each week, and wants to estimate the number that will have 8 or more flaws.\par \textbf{c} Explain why an estimate based on the observed relative frequencies would not be useful.\par \textbf{d} Use a Poisson distribution to estimate the number of pieces of cloth with 8 or more flaws.

\textbf{a} Let $x$ be the number of flaws on a piece of cloth and $f$ its frequency. The total frequency is $8+19+28+25+19+11+7+3=120$.\par $\sum fx=8(0)+19(1)+28(2)+25(3)+19(4)+11(5)+7(6)+3(7)=344$.\par $\bar x=\dfrac{\sum fx}{\sum f}=\dfrac{344}{120}=2.867$ (3 d.p.).\par $\sum fx^2=8(0^2)+19(1^2)+28(2^2)+25(3^2)$\par $\qquad+19(4^2)+11(5^2)+7(6^2)+3(7^2)=1334$.\par $\sigma^2=\dfrac{\sum fx^2}{\sum f}-\bar x^2=\dfrac{1334}{120}-\left(\dfrac{344}{120}\right)^2=2.899$ (3 d.p.).\par \textbf{b} The mean and variance both round to $2.9$ (1 d.p.). A Poisson variable has equal mean and variance, so these data support a Poisson model.\par \textbf{c} None of the 120 pieces had eight or more flaws. Scaling the observed proportion $0/120$ up to 10 000 pieces gives zero. The sample is too small to estimate this rare event reliably. Such pieces can still occur.\par \textbf{d} Following the scheme, estimate $\lambda=2.9$. With $X\sim\operatorname{Po}(2.9)$, a calculator gives $\mathrm P(X\ge8)=1-\mathrm P(X\le7)\approx1-0.9901=0.0099$.\par The estimated number is $10\,000\times0.0099=99$ pieces.

Tests for flaws are carried out in a textile factory on a consignment of 120 pieces of cloth. The results of the tests are shown in the table.\par $\begin{array}{l|rrrrrrrrr}\text{Number of flaws}&0&1&2&3&4&5&6&7&\ge8\\\hline\text{Number of pieces}&8&19&28&25&19&11&7&3&0\end{array}$

transcription.tex: Question 8

A sweet company produces chocolate-covered wafer biscuit bars. The probability of a bar being solid chocolate is 0.04.\par \textbf{a} Find the probability that in a box of 48 bars, at least two are solid chocolate.\par The company produces 120 boxes of biscuits per day.\par \textbf{b} Find the mean and variance of the number of boxes of biscuits which contain at least two solid chocolate bars.

\textbf{a} Let $X$ count solid chocolate bars in a box. Then $X\sim\operatorname{B}(48,0.04)$. Using a calculator,\par $p=\mathrm P(X\ge2)=1-\mathrm P(X\le1)\approx1-0.4228=0.5772$.\par \textbf{b} Let $Y$ count qualifying boxes among the 120 boxes that day. Assuming independent boxes, $Y\sim\operatorname{B}(120,p)$. Using the tabulated precision from part (a),\par $\mathrm E(Y)=120p\approx120(0.5772)=69.264$.\par $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=120p(1-p)\approx120(0.5772)(1-0.5772)$\par $=120(0.5772)(0.4228)\approx29.28$ (2 d.p.).
Question 9

The random variable $X$ is such that $X\sim\operatorname{B}(5,p)$. Given that $\mathrm P(X\ge1)=0.83193$, find:\par \textbf{a} the value of $p$\par \textbf{b} $\mathrm E(X)$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)$.

\textbf{a} Since $X\sim\operatorname{B}(5,p)$, $\mathrm P(X\ge1)=1-\mathrm P(X=0)$.\par $1-\binom50p^0(1-p)^5=1-(1-p)^5=0.83193$.\par Hence $(1-p)^5=1-0.83193=0.16807$. Taking the fifth root gives $1-p=0.7$, so $p=0.3$.\par \textbf{b} $\mathrm E(X)=np=5(0.3)=1.5$.\par $\operatorname{Var}(X)=np(1-p)=5(0.3)(0.7)=1.05$.

Question 11

Each cell of a certain insect contains 1200 genes. It is known that each gene has a probability 0.005 of being damaged. A cell is chosen at random.\par \textbf{a} Suggest a suitable model for the distribution of the number of damaged genes in the cell.\par \textbf{b} Find the mean and variance of the number of damaged genes in the cell.\par \textbf{c} Using a Poisson approximation, find the probability that there are at most 4 damaged genes in the cell.

\textbf{a} Let $X$ count damaged genes in the cell. Assuming damage occurs independently with the same probability for each gene, $X\sim\operatorname{B}(1200,0.005)$.\par \textbf{b} $\mathrm E(X)=np=1200(0.005)=6$.\par $\operatorname{Var}(X)=np(1-p)=1200(0.005)(0.995)=5.97$.\par \textbf{c} With large $n$ and small $p$, use $Z\sim\operatorname{Po}(1200\times0.005)=\operatorname{Po}(6)$ to approximate $X$. From the tables, $\mathrm P(X\le4)\approx\mathrm P(Z\le4)=0.2851$ (4 d.p.).
Question 12

A machine which manufactures nails is known to produce 2.5% defective nails. The nails are sold in packets of 200.\par \textbf{a} Using a Poisson approximation, calculate the probability that a packet contains more than 6 defective nails.\par A carpenter buys 6 packets of nails.\par \textbf{b} Estimate the probability that more than half of these packets contain more than 6 defective nails.

\textbf{a} Let $X$ count defective nails in a packet. $X\sim\operatorname{B}(200,0.025)$. Approximate with $Z\sim\operatorname{Po}(200\times0.025)=\operatorname{Po}(5)$.\par Using the tables, $p=\mathrm P(X>6)\approx1-\mathrm P(Z\le6)=1-0.7622=0.2378$.\par \textbf{b} Let $Y$ count packets containing more than 6 defective nails. Treat the six packets as independent, so $Y\sim\operatorname{B}(6,p)$.\par More than half means at least four of the six packets. A calculator gives $\mathrm P(Y>3)=1-\mathrm P(Y\le3)\approx1-0.9685=0.0315$ (4 d.p.).
Question 13

The probability of an electrical component being defective is 0.0125. The component is supplied in boxes of 400.\par \textbf{a} Using a Poisson approximation, estimate the probability that there are more than 3 defective components in a box.\par A retailer buys 5 boxes of components.\par \textbf{b} Estimate the probability that there are more than 3 defective components in 3 of the boxes.

\textbf{a} Let $X$ count defective components in one box. $X\sim\operatorname{B}(400,0.0125)$. Approximate with $Z\sim\operatorname{Po}(400\times0.0125)=\operatorname{Po}(5)$.\par From the tables, $p=\mathrm P(X>3)\approx1-\mathrm P(Z\le3)=1-0.2650=0.7350$.\par \textbf{b} Let $Y$ count boxes containing more than 3 defective components. With independent boxes, $Y\sim\operatorname{B}(5,p)$.\par $\mathrm P(Y=3)=\binom53p^3(1-p)^2\approx\binom53(0.735)^3(0.265)^2=0.2788$ (4 d.p.).
Question 14

It is claimed that 95% of the letters posted 1st class arrive the next day. Based on this claim, calculate, using a Poisson approximation, the probability that in a sample of 180 letters,\par \textbf{a} more than 173 arrive the day after posting\par \textbf{b} fewer than 168 arrive the day after posting.

\textbf{a} Let $X$ count letters arriving the next day. Work with the rarer outcome. $Y=180-X$ counts letters that arrive late. With independent deliveries, $Y\sim\operatorname{B}(180,0.05)$.\par Approximate $Y$ by $Z\sim\operatorname{Po}(180\times0.05)=\operatorname{Po}(9)$.\par More than 173 timely letters means at most 6 late ones. From the tables, $\mathrm P(X>173)=\mathrm P(Y\le6)\approx\mathrm P(Z\le6)=0.2068$.\par \textbf{b} Fewer than 168 timely letters means more than 12 late ones.\par $\mathrm P(X<168)=\mathrm P(Y>12)\approx1-\mathrm P(Z\le12)=1-0.8758=0.1242$.
Question 15

A farmer supplies a bakery with eggs. The manager of the bakery claims that the proportion of eggs which are broken on delivery is 1%. The farmer supplies the eggs to the bakery on a daily basis in consignments of 150 eggs.\par \textbf{a} Based on the claim of the manager, calculate, using a Poisson approximation, the probability that a consignment contains more than 4 broken eggs.\par The farmer supplies a consignment to the baker on 5 days every week.\par \textbf{b} Calculate the probability that in a particular week one of the consignments contains more than 4 broken eggs.

\textbf{a} Let $X$ count broken eggs in one consignment. Under the claim, $X\sim\operatorname{B}(150,0.01)$. Approximate with $Z\sim\operatorname{Po}(150\times0.01)=\operatorname{Po}(1.5)$.\par From the tables, $p=\mathrm P(X>4)\approx1-\mathrm P(Z\le4)=1-0.9814=0.0186$.\par \textbf{b} Let $Y$ count consignments containing more than 4 broken eggs among the five independent deliveries in a week. Then $Y\sim\operatorname{B}(5,p)$.\par $\mathrm P(Y=1)=\binom51p(1-p)^4\approx\binom51(0.0186)^1(0.9814)^4=0.0863$ (4 d.p.).

slides.title: Appendix · Proof of the Poisson probability formula

transcription.tex: Fix a non-negative integer $x$ and take $p=\lambda/n$. Prove that the binomial probability tends to $e^{-\lambda}\lambda^x/x!$.
$\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\binom nx\left(\frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^x\left(1-\frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^{n-x}$

Expand $\binom nx=n(n-1)\cdots(n-x+1)/x!$.\par $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\dfrac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-x+1)}{x!}\,\dfrac{\lambda^x}{n^x}\left(1-\frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^{n-x}$.\par Dividing the $x$ factors by $n$ gives $1(1-\tfrac1n)(1-\tfrac2n)\cdots(1-\tfrac{x-1}{n})$. Their product tends to 1 because $x$ is fixed.

$\displaystyle\left(1-\frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^{n-x}=\dfrac{(1-\lambda/n)^n}{(1-\lambda/n)^x}\longrightarrow\dfrac{e^{-\lambda}}{1}=e^{-\lambda}$.\par The numerator uses the standard exponential limit. The denominator tends to 1 for fixed $x$.\par Therefore $\displaystyle\mathrm P(X=x)=\boxed{\dfrac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^x}{x!}}$.
